claim: Individual responses to anesthetics dynamically fluctuate at a fixed drug concentration.
source: Individual responses dynamically fluctuated at a fixed drug concentration.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing fluctuations in righting reflex in mice and startle reflex in zebrafish at constant anesthetic concentrations (Figures 2A, 2C).

claim: Fluctuations in responsiveness exhibit resistance to state transitions.
source: These fluctuations exhibited resistance to state transitions.
evidence: Data shows that animals are more likely to remain in their current state than transition between responsive and unresponsive states (Figures 3G, 3H).

claim: Drug sensitivity varies dramatically across individuals in both mice and zebrafish.
source: Drug sensitivity varied dramatically across individuals in both species.
evidence: Experimental data demonstrates high inter-individual variability in response probabilities at fixed anesthetic concentrations (Figures 3C, 3D, 4C, 4E).

claim: The amount of noise driving transitions between states is highly conserved in vertebrates separated by 400 million years of evolution.
source: The amount of noise driving transitions between states, in contrast, was highly conserved in vertebrates separated by 400 million years of evolution.
evidence: Analysis shows strong negative correlation between P(U|U) and P(R|R) in both mice and zebrafish, indicating conserved noise levels (Figures 4C, 4E).

claim: At 0.6% isoflurane, the probability of an intact righting reflex was 44 ± 6% (mean ± SD across trials) after 2 hours of equilibration.
source: After 2 hr of equilibration at 0.6% isoflurane, the probability of an intact RR was 44 ± 6% (mean ± SD across trials).
evidence: Direct measurement from experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In every mouse, the outcome of the righting reflex test fluctuated over time at a fixed anesthetic concentration.
source: Instead, in every mouse, the outcome of the RR test fluctuated over time at a fixed anesthetic concentration (Figure 2A)
evidence: Figure 2A shows fluctuations between responsive and unresponsive states in all 20 mice tested.

claim: Population response probability at 0.6% isoflurane remained stable over time.
source: while the population response probability at 0.6% isoflurane remained stable over time (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows R2 = 4.3×10−16, p=1 for correlation between trial number and response probability.

claim: Individual larval zebrafish demonstrated fluctuating responses to identical tap stimuli at 3 μM propofol.
source: Individual larval zebrafish demonstrated fluctuating responses to identical tap stimuli (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows fluctuations in startle reflex responses across 72 zebrafish.

claim: The response probability across the zebrafish population remained constant at 45 ± 5% (mean ± SD across trials) for three hours after an initial hour of equilibration in 3 μM propofol.
source: The response probability across the population remained constant (45 ± 5% mean ± SD across trials) for three hours after an initial hour of equilibration in 3 μM propofol (Figure 2D).
evidence: Figure 2D shows stable population response probability with R2 = 1.2×10−14, p=1.

claim: Experimentally observed switches between positive and negative righting reflex occur less frequently than in a Bernoulli process simulation.
source: Note, however, that the experimentally observed switches between positive and negative RR occur less frequently than in the simulation (Figure 3E, U = 48.5, nsim = nexp = 20, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical comparison between experimental data and Bernoulli simulations shows significant difference in transition frequency.

claim: In mice, the probability of being unresponsive on the next trial was significantly higher if the animal was found to be unresponsive on the preceding trial.
source: In both mice (Figure 3G, U = 103, nP(U|R) = nP(U|U)=20, p<0.001) and zebrafish (Figure 3H, U = 501, nP(U|R) = nP(U|U)=72, p<0.0001), the probability of being unresponsive on the next trial was significantly higher if the animal was found to be unresponsive on the preceding trial.
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing P(U|U) to P(U|R) shows significant difference in both species.

claim: Experimentally observed inter-individual variability in responsiveness was significantly higher than in simulations constrained to have the same number of trials.
source: Experimentally observed inter-individual variability was significantly higher than in simulations constrained to have the same number of trials (Figure 3C, F(1, 38)=27.8, p<0.0001 for mice, Figure 3D, F(1,142)=52.5, p<0.0001 for zebrafish, Brown-Forsythe test).
evidence: Brown-Forsythe test comparing experimental and simulated variance shows significant differences.

claim: The dwell times in responsive and unresponsive states for both mice and zebrafish were approximately exponential.
source: The dwell times in responsive and unresponsive states for both mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) were approximately exponential.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B show dwell time distributions on semi-log scale.

claim: No significant autocorrelations in fluctuations were observed in mice or zebrafish.
source: No significant autocorrelations in fluctuations were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Autocorrelation functions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D demonstrate lack of significant autocorrelation.

claim: P(U|U) and P(R|R) are strongly negatively correlated among individual mice (R2 = −0.85, p<0.0001).
source: Therefore, P(U|U) and P(R|R) are strongly negatively correlated among individuals (R2 = −0.85, p<0.0001, Pearson's R).
evidence: Statistical analysis of transition probability matrices estimated for individual mice shows strong negative correlation (Figure 4C).

claim: P(U|U) and P(R|R) are strongly negatively correlated among individual zebrafish (R2 = −0.77, p<0.0001).
source: The same relationship was observed in larval zebrafish (Figure 4E, R2 = −0.77, p<0.0001, Pearson's R).
evidence: Statistical analysis of transition probability matrices estimated for individual zebrafish shows strong negative correlation.

claim: The amount of noise that drives state transitions between responsive and unresponsive states was consistent in all individuals exposed to a fixed anesthetic concentration.
source: The fact that their sum is constant across individuals implies that the amount of noise that drives state transitions between responsive and unresponsive states was consistent in all individuals exposed to a fixed anesthetic concentration.
evidence: The negative correlation between P(U|U) and P(R|R) implies conservation of their sum, which relates to noise levels.

claim: There is significant overlap (57%) in response probability distributions between mice exposed to 0.3% and 0.6% isoflurane.
source: Note, however, that there is significant overlap (57%) between the two distributions.
evidence: Analysis of response probability distributions at two different isoflurane concentrations shows 57% overlap (Figure 6B).

claim: It is not possible to reliably determine whether an individual mouse was exposed to 0.6% or 0.3% isoflurane over a large range of individual anesthetic sensitivities.
source: As a consequence of this overlap, it is not possible to reliably determine whether an individual was exposed to 0.6% or 0.3% isoflurane over a large range of individual anesthetic sensitivities (Figure 6C).
evidence: Posterior probability distributions shown in Figure 6C demonstrate near-chance classification over a broad range of response probabilities.

claim: Individual transition probability matrices estimated separately for the first two and the last two exposures to 0.6% isoflurane in mice were correlated (R2 = 0.50, p=0.025).
source: In mice, individual transition probability matrices estimated separately for the first two and the last two exposures to 0.6% isoflurane were correlated (R2 = 0.50, p=0.025, Pearson's R ).
evidence: Figure 5A shows correlation between transition probability matrices estimated at different time points.

claim: Individual transition probability matrices estimated separately for the first and second halves of propofol exposure in zebrafish were correlated (R2 = 0.53, p<0.0001).
source: In zebrafish, individual transition probability matrices estimated separately for the first and second halves of the exposure to 3 μM propofol were correlated (R2 = 0.53, p<0.0001, Pearson's R ).
evidence: Figure 5B shows correlation between transition probability matrices estimated at different time points.

claim: MAC-awake and the EC50 for loss of righting reflex are closely correlated across mechanistically distinct anesthetics.
source: MAC-awake and the EC50 for loss of RR are closely correlated across mechanistically distinct anesthetics (Franks, 2008).
evidence: Citation to published work by Franks (2008) supports this relationship.

claim: Anesthesia is thought to consist of four basic components: amnesia, immobility, analgesia, and unconsciousness.
source: Anesthesia is thought to consist of four basic components: amnesia, immobility, analgesia, and unconsciousness.
evidence: This is established knowledge in anesthesiology.

claim: At lower anesthetic doses that produce light sedation, a patient can respond to salient verbal commands and less noticeable auditory commands, albeit with longer latency.
source: At lower anesthetic doses that produce light sedation, a patient can respond to salient verbal commands and less noticeable auditory commands (Wong et al., 2014), albeit with longer latency.
evidence: Citation to Wong et al., 2014 supports this clinical observation.

claim: When the state of general anesthesia is attained, the patient is unresponsive even to a painful surgical stimulus.
source: When the state of general anesthesia is attained, the patient is unresponsive even to a painful surgical stimulus (Miller, 2014).
evidence: Citation to Miller, 2014 supports this clinical definition.

claim: Approximately ten percent of patients transiently wake up during surgery as measured by their ability to respond to a verbal command.
source: Nonetheless, approximately ten percent of patients transiently wake up during surgery as measured by their ability to respond to a verbal command (Sanders et al., 2017; Russell, 2013; Gaskell et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to Sanders et al., 2017; Russell, 2013; Gaskell et al., 2017 support this clinical observation.

claim: Hill slopes of dose-response curves for anesthetics are reported between 10 and 40.
source: On the one hand, Hill slopes of dose-response curves for anesthetics are reported between 10 and 40 (Miller, 2014); some of the steepest of the clinically used drugs.
evidence: Citation to Miller, 2014 provides published Hill slope values.

claim: The Hill slope value observed in this study was approximately an order of magnitude lower than previously published data.
source: The Hill slope value observed in our study was approximately an order of magnitude lower than the previously published data (Friedman et al., 2010; Joiner et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison between current study results and cited previous work shows difference in Hill slope estimates.

claim: The EC50 estimate for isoflurane in this study (0.54–0.55%) is significantly lower than that published in previous work (0.9% for induction and 0.83% for emergence).
source: Indeed, our EC50 estimate (0.54–0.55% isoflurane) is significantly lower than that published in the previous work (0.9% for induction and 0.83% for emergence) (Friedman et al., 2010).
evidence: Comparison of EC50 values between current study and cited work by Friedman et al., 2010.

claim: Anesthetics at least in part hijack the sleep-wake circuitry by exciting sleep-promoting and inhibiting wake-promoting neurons.
source: A number of lines of evidence converge on the fact that anesthetics at least in part hijack the sleep-wake circuitry by exciting sleep-promoting and inhibiting wake-promoting neurons (Zhang et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2012; Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014; Nelson et al., 2002).
evidence: Multiple citations support this mechanistic understanding of anesthetic action.

claim: Switching between sleep and wake is thought to be mediated by the reciprocal inhibition between sleep-promoting and wake-promoting neuronal populations.
source: Switching between sleep and wake is thought to be mediated by the reciprocal inhibition between these neuronal populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sleep-wake circuitry, supported by the broader context of cited literature.

claim: At a fixed anesthetic concentration, spectral characteristics of electrical activity within thalamocortical networks switch stochastically between several discrete activity patterns.
source: Our observations of stochastic switching between responsive and unresponsive states are consistent with previous findings showing that at a fixed anesthetic concentration, spectral characteristics of electrical activity within thalamocortical networks switch stochastically between several discrete activity patterns (Hudson et al., 2014; Clement et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations to Hudson et al., 2014 and Clement et al., 2008 support this observation.

claim: Similar observations of stochastic switching have been made using electroencephalography (EEG) of patients under anesthesia.
source: Similar observations have been made using electroencephalography (EEG) of patients under anesthesia (Chander et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Vlisides et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to Chander et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Vlisides et al., 2019 support this clinical observation.

claim: Anesthetics stabilize neuronal dynamics in humans.
source: It has been suggested previously that anesthetics stabilize neuronal dynamics in humans (Alonso et al., 2014; Tagliazucchi et al., 2016) and in non-human primates (Solovey et al., 2015; Alonso et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to multiple studies support this observation across species.

claim: Stabilization of neuronal dynamics may contribute to the behavioral inertia observed in fluctuations in responsiveness of both mice and zebrafish.
source: Stabilization of neuronal dynamics may contribute to the behavioral inertia observed in fluctuations in responsiveness of both mice and zebrafish.
evidence: This is an inference connecting cited observations about neuronal dynamics to the behavioral findings in the current study.

claim: Resistance to state transitions may contribute to anesthetic hysteresis.
source: This resistance to state transitions may contribute (Proekt and Hudson, 2018) to anesthetic hysteresis (Friedman et al., 2010; Joiner et al., 2013; Kuizenga et al., 2018; Warnaby et al., 2017)
evidence: Citation to Proekt and Hudson, 2018 and multiple other studies support this connection.

claim: Anesthetic hysteresis is a left-shift in a dose-response curve for emergence relative to induction of anesthesia that has been observed across taxa from Drosophila to humans.
source: anesthetic hysteresis (Friedman et al., 2010; Joiner et al., 2013; Kuizenga et al., 2018; Warnaby et al., 2017) – a left-shift in a dose-response curve for emergence relative to induction of anesthesia that has been observed across taxa from Drosophila to humans.
evidence: Multiple citations support this phenomenon across species.

claim: Tolerance to repeated isoflurane exposures does not occur.
source: As tolerance to repeated isoflurane exposures does not occur (Smith et al., 1979), mice were exposed to each isoflurane concentration a total of four times over the course of 3 weeks.
evidence: Citation to Smith et al., 1979 supports the lack of tolerance to repeated isoflurane exposures.

claim: Target volatile anesthetic concentrations were reached within 5 minutes of drug exposure onset.
source: Target volatile anesthetic concentrations were reached within 5 min of drug exposure onset.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows chamber equilibration data.

claim: Zebrafish exposed to no propofol had a significantly higher response probability to the tap stimulus than those exposed to 3 μM propofol (U = 55, nE3 = n3µM=360 trials, p<0.0001).
source: Zebrafish exposed to no propofol had a significantly higher response probability to the tap stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, U = 55, nE3 = n3µM=360 trials, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical comparison between control and propofol-exposed zebrafish shows significant difference.

claim: Drug concentration remained constant in the propofol exposures.
source: Drug concentration remained constant in the propofol exposures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2B shows propofol concentration measurements over time.

claim: The distribution of velocities elicited by a tap stimulus in zebrafish is bimodal.
source: Distribution of velocities elicited by a tap stimulus is bimodal.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2C shows bimodal distribution of distances travelled.

claim: At the population level, distributions of responsiveness at 0.4% and 0.7% isoflurane are significantly different (U = 7, n0.4% iso = n0.7% iso = 20, p<0.0001).
source: At the population level, distributions of responsiveness at the two isoflurane concentrations are significantly different (U = 7, n 0.4% iso = n 0.7% iso = 20, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of response probabilities at two isoflurane concentrations in the same mice.

claim: Overlap of response probabilities at the population level between 0.4% and 0.7% isoflurane was 18%.
source: Overlap of the two distributions was 18%.
evidence: Analysis of response probability distributions shows 18% overlap (Figure 7A).

claim: Overlap at the individual level between 0.4% and 0.7% isoflurane varied widely, from close to zero to nearly complete.
source: Overlap at the individual level varied widely, from close to zero to nearly complete (Figure 7B,C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figures 7B, 7C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 show variable overlap across individual mice.

claim: Observing the same individual exposed to different drug concentrations improves the reliability of distinguishing between drug concentrations on the basis of righting probability.
source: Thus, observing the same individual exposed to different drug concentrations, improves the reliability of distinguishing between drug concentrations on the basis of righting probability.
evidence: Comparison of overlap between within-subject (18%) and between-subject (57%) designs shows improvement.

claim: In order to reproduce the experimental results, the amount of noise in the bistable network model needs to be tuned and maintained at approximately the same level across individuals.
source: In order to reproduce the results in Figures 4 and 6, the amount of noise needs to be tuned and maintained at an approximately the same level across individuals.
evidence: Modeling results in Figure 8D demonstrate that matching experimental data requires conserved noise levels.

claim: In the bistable network simulations, Gaussian noise with mean 0 and standard deviation (σ)=0.4 reproduces the experimental results.
source: In the simulations, this corresponds to Gaussian noise with mean 0 and standard deviation (σ)=0.4.
evidence: Modeling analysis identifies specific noise parameter that matches experimental observations.

claim: While individuals are different in terms of anesthetic sensitivity, the amount of noise that drives fluctuations between the responsive and the unresponsive states is conserved.
source: These simulations support our conjecture that while individuals are different in terms of anesthetic sensitivity, the amount of noise that drives fluctuations between the responsive and the unresponsive states is conserved.
evidence: Modeling results combined with experimental data support this conclusion.

claim: In units of trial number, the dwell time distributions were similar in fish and in mice.
source: Note, that in the units of trial number, the dwell time distributions were similar in fish and in mice.
evidence: Comparison of dwell time distributions across species shows similarity when measured in trial units.

claim: In units of seconds, mice dwelled significantly longer in the awake and the unresponsive state than zebrafish.
source: However, in mice the trials were spaced 3 minutes apart whereas in fish the inter-trial interval was 30 seconds. Thus, in units of seconds, mice dwelled signficantly longer in the awake and the unresponsive state than zebrafish.
evidence: Comparison of inter-trial intervals reveals species difference in absolute dwell times.

claim: The duration of responsive and unresponsive states was approximately similar to the duration of sleep episodes in mice and zebrafish.
source: The duration of responsive and unresponsive states was approximately similar to the duration of sleep episodes in these two species (Zhang et al., 2007; Yokogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to Zhang et al., 2007 and Yokogawa et al., 2007 provide comparison data on sleep episode durations.

claim: It is possible that the relationship between duration of sleep episodes and the duration of the episodes of unresponsiveness arises because similar neurobiological mechanisms are responsible for both transitions between sleep and wakefulness and fluctuations between the responsive and the unresponsive states observed under anesthesia.
source: It is possible that this relationship between duration of sleep episodes and the duration of the episodes of unresponsiveness arises because similar neurobiological mechanisms are responsible for both transitions between sleep and wakefulness and fluctuations between the responsive and the unresponsive states observed under anesthesia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed similarity in dwell times.

claim: Interference with orexinergic signaling destabilizes both sleep and wake states thereby increasing the frequency of spontaneous transitions between sleep and wakefulness.
source: For instance, interference with orexinergic signaling destabilizes both sleep and wake states thereby increasing the frequency of spontaneous transitions between sleep and wakefulness (Mochizuki et al., 2004).
evidence: Citation to Mochizuki et al., 2004 supports this observation about orexin's role.

claim: Interference with orexin signaling affects responses to anesthetics.
source: Interestingly, interference with orexin signaling also affects responses to anesthetics (Kelz et al., 2008; Shirasaka et al., 2011; Tose et al., 2009; Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: Multiple citations support the effect of orexin signaling on anesthetic responses.

claim: Detailed investigation of the synergy between anesthetics and modification of noise inherent in neuronal networks that control sleep and wakefulness may help develop novel therapies that will allow clinicians better control over the state of each individual patient.
source: Detailed investigation of the synergy between anesthetics and modification of noise inherent in neuronal networks that control sleep and wakefulness may help develop novel therapies that will allow clinicians better control over the state of each individual patient.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future therapeutic applications.

claim: Selective stabilization of the unconscious state could provide a solution to minimize the risk of spontaneously shifting into a brain state where awareness is possible, without requiring drug concentrations prone to adverse effects.
source: Selective stabilization of the unconscious state could provide a solution to minimize the risk of spontaneously shifting into a brain state where awareness is possible, without requiring drug concentrations prone to adverse effects.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for a therapeutic approach based on the study findings.

claim: Individual differences in anesthetic sensitivity and stochastic fluctuations in responsiveness complicate the ability to appropriately dose anesthetics to each individual.
source: Individual differences in anesthetic sensitivity and stochastic fluctuations in responsiveness complicate the ability to appropriately dose anesthetics to each individual.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing inter-individual variability and stochastic fluctuations.

claim: Identifying the biological substrate of noise may spur novel therapies, assure consistent drug responses, and encourage the shift from population-based to personalized medicine.
source: Identifying the biological substrate of noise, however, may spur novel therapies, assure consistent drug responses, and encourage the shift from population-based to personalized medicine.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of understanding noise mechanisms.

claim: Population-based dose-response curves cannot be used to reliably determine the probability that any given individual will (or will not) be anesthetized.
source: As a result of the inter-subject variability and stochastic intra-subject fluctuations in responsiveness, the population-level concentration response cannot be used to reliably determine the probability that any given individual will (or will not) be anesthetized.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing overlap in response probabilities at different drug concentrations.

claim: Detailed quantification of stochastic forces that shape the within-subject fluctuations in responsiveness and between-subject variability lays the foundation for the construction of more informative stochastic models.
source: Detailed quantification of stochastic forces that shape the within-subject fluctuations in responsiveness and between-subject variability lays the foundation for the construction of more informative stochastic models that can reconcile binary responses of individual organisms with population-based measures of drug potency.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the study's quantitative approach.

claim: These models can be used to deliver on the promise of personalized medicine to deliver the appropriate dose of medication tailored to each individual patient.
source: These models can in turn be used to deliver on the promise of personalized medicine to deliver the appropriate dose of medication tailored to each individual patient.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the modeling approach.
